# Use AI to widen the search, not choose the research bet

[Visual: A narrow search box expands into a branching map of candidate research questions.]

A language model can produce twenty dissertation ideas before you finish your coffee. That is useful—but it is not originality. The valuable question is whether AI can enlarge the space you examine without deciding which intellectual risk you should take.

The strongest case for AI-assisted discovery comes from structured search, not one-shot prompting. In a Nature Machine Intelligence study of combinatorial optimization, the LACE framework divided algorithm design into a verified problem contract, tool library, and portfolio of candidate heuristics. Across 36 benchmark problems, its authors reported an average score of 0.945. The strongest compared LLM-based method scored 0.870, while direct prompting scored 0.571. [claim:01-c1]

[Visual: Three labeled bars—LACE 0.945, strongest LLM baseline 0.870, direct prompting 0.571. Caption: “Reported on 36 CO-Bench problems.”]

This does not show that LACE can choose a dissertation topic. The benchmarks were bounded optimization problems, all LLM-based methods shared one model backbone, and the framework’s authors conducted its evaluation. But the comparison illustrates a transferable principle: models become more useful when a researcher defines constraints, decomposes the search, tests candidates, and iterates.

A Nature commentary describes a related approach to evidence exploration. It highlights staged searching, an evolving evidence graph, and a checklist revised as new findings arrive, instead of commitment after one retrieval pass. [claim:01-c3]

[Visual: Loop diagram: Plan → Search → Record evidence → Replan. Beside it, citations accumulate in a provenance graph.]

For topic discovery, that suggests a practical workflow. Ask AI to generate candidates across different assumptions, methods, datasets, and application areas. Require it to state what evidence would establish novelty, what could falsify the premise, and which dependencies require checking. Then trace every promising claim to primary literature. An evidence graph can improve traceability; it cannot establish that a question is correct, feasible, or important.

The human role is not merely supervisory. MIT professor Alexander Rakhlin argues that routine calculations, coding, failed approaches, and small discoveries help graduate students develop intuition and judgment. In his account, delegating such work can remove formative experiences even while AI enables more ambitious projects. [claim:01-c2]

[Visual: Split screen. Left: “avoidable friction.” Right: “practice that builds judgment.” A researcher decides where each task belongs.]

Problem choice also reflects values and incentives. In a Latent Space interview, MIT researcher Alex Zhang associates distinctive academic work with questions that industry may not be pursuing, while warning that graduate students can gravitate toward topics attractive to industry labs. That is practitioner testimony, not controlled evidence, and the technology-focused publisher benefits from interest in agent systems. Still, it identifies a real question to ask: Is this topic important because of the underlying science—or because it fits today’s benchmark economy? [claim:01-c4]

The danger of scale is visible when generation outruns checking. Retraction Watch reported that a sign error in one AI-produced mathematics manuscript invalidated its argument and constructions used by two dependent papers. This case does not estimate the general error rate of AI-assisted research, but it shows how one unchecked dependency can propagate. [claim:01-c5]

[Visual: One red error node feeds three manuscript cards. Avoid depicting any broader error rate.]

So use AI to widen the search. Have it challenge assumptions, expose neighboring literatures, generate counterarguments, and organize evidence. But reserve three decisions for accountable scholarly judgment: whether the problem matters, whether the contribution is genuinely novel, and whether the evidence supports proceeding.

Human control is no guarantee of originality; people are also conservative and biased. The defensible division of labor is narrower: AI expands and tests possibilities inside explicit constraints. The researcher chooses the bet—and remains responsible for verifying it. [claim:01-c5]

- Use abstract search maps, article pages, checklists, and researcher-created notes. Do not imply access to unpublished topic-success or error-rate data.

# Replace one-shot drafting with a verified research pipeline

[Visual: A polished paragraph appears instantly, then dissolves into a pipeline of sources, tests, revisions, and approvals.]

The wrong unit of AI assistance is the generated paragraph. A fluent paragraph can conceal a false citation, a broken computation, or a dependency nobody checked. The more defensible unit is a verified workflow: explicit inputs, tools, tests, provenance, and revision.

Evidence from algorithm design shows why structure matters. The LACE framework gives a language model a verified problem contract, tool library, repair operations, and an iterative process for generating and selecting heuristics. On its combinatorial-optimization benchmark, LACE achieved a reported Valid Rate of 0.944; none of the compared LLM-based baselines exceeded 0.611. Valid Rate measured whether an algorithm produced feasible solutions for every test instance of a problem. [claim:02-c1]

[Visual: Labeled comparison—LACE Valid Rate 0.944; other LLM baselines no higher than 0.611. Caption: “CO-Bench feasibility metric.”]

That is not a controlled study of academic prose. But it demonstrates the advantage of surrounding generation with constraints, executable tools, evaluation, selection, and repair. For writing, the corresponding pipeline begins before drafting.

First, define the claim. Record what kind of support it needs: a primary study, a theorem, a dataset, or a computation. Second, let AI search, classify, compare, or propose wording. Third, verify the underlying source or run the test. Fourth, record the dependency. Only then should the claim enter the manuscript.

[Visual: Five gates: Claim → Required evidence → AI assistance → Verification → Manuscript.]

The cost of ignoring dependencies appears in a reported mathematics release. According to Retraction Watch, OpenAI withdrew three AI-produced manuscripts after a sign error invalidated an argument in one paper and constructions used by two dependent papers. The company also reported revisions to 14 other manuscripts, including proof repairs, corrected statements, clearer hypotheses and dependencies, and one obsolete-citation correction. [claim:02-c2]

This is one unusually large release, not a base-rate estimate for AI-assisted scholarship. Retraction Watch also reported OpenAI’s statement that roughly half of the results had been released unconfirmed. The episode nevertheless shows why verification cannot be postponed until after hundreds of polished outputs exist.

Citation checking needs the same discipline. In a SciSpace webinar, a journal and grant reviewer advises checking every AI-supplied DOI to ensure it resolves to the work it claims to identify. [claim:02-c3]

[Visual: A DOI is opened. Title, authors, venue, year, and cited proposition are checked one by one.]

Resolving the link is only the first test. The researcher must still confirm that the paper exists, the metadata match, and the source actually supports the sentence. SciSpace sells research software, so this is practitioner guidance rather than independent validation of its products. The procedure itself is straightforward and auditable.

Provenance can extend beyond citations. In a Latent Space interview, representatives of Periodic Labs say their system records conversations, intuitions, laboratory actions, computations, and code. Their stated goal is to train on the process of science rather than only its final output. [claim:02-c4]

[Visual: A laboratory timeline connects discussion notes, code commits, computation records, failed trials, and final results.]

Periodic Labs is describing a commercial platform, not presenting a controlled comparison. Still, the lineage principle transfers: keep the failed query, changed assumption, source excerpt, script version, and reason for accepting or rejecting a result. Privacy, security, confidential review, and proprietary-data rules may limit what can be logged, so provenance must be designed around those obligations.

Across these cases, the evidence supports an inference, not a universal guarantee: efficiency and rigor are more compatible when tests and provenance are embedded in every iteration. A polished output alone is not a quality-control signal. [claim:02-c5]

Use AI where it reduces search and revision costs. But make every externally checkable claim point to a source, every computational result point to an executable test, and every important dependency visible before submission.

# Authorship after AI: responsibility cannot be delegated

[Visual: A manuscript’s “Generate” button changes into four questions: Can you verify it? Reproduce it? Defend it? Correct it?]

AI can search, draft, code, and propose arguments. It cannot assume authorship responsibility. If your name is on the paper, you still need to know what the evidence supports, how the result was produced, and what must happen if the result fails.

That responsibility begins with a distinction between a plausible derivation and a faithful account of model behavior. A Nature Machine Intelligence perspective called “State over Tokens” argues that model-generated reasoning text may explain how an answer could follow through a sequence of steps without explaining the actual process that produced the answer. [claim:03-c1]

[Visual: Two paths reach the same answer. One is labeled “plausible derivation”; the hidden model process remains marked “not established.”]

This does not make every displayed derivation useless. A reader may still inspect individual steps. The warning is about trust calibration: fluent reasoning can increase confidence without justifying it. So do not treat a model’s rationale as a faithful audit log merely because it sounds systematic.

Authorship must therefore be grounded elsewhere—in evidence, reproducibility, and identifiable decisions. MIT professor Alexander Rakhlin argues that academic evaluation should determine what a researcher contributed and takes intellectual responsibility for, including when substantial parts of the work were performed by AI. [claim:03-c2]

[Visual: Contribution record with columns for question formulation, source verification, computation, interpretation, and final approval.]

That standard is more useful than counting keystrokes. A researcher might type little yet make the decisive conceptual and evidentiary contributions. Another might edit every sentence while failing to understand the derivation. Responsible authorship asks whether the named researcher can reproduce the work, defend its assumptions, explain its dependencies, and identify what the AI contributed.

The stakes become clearer at scale. Retraction Watch reported that OpenAI said roughly half the results in a release of more than 700 mathematics manuscripts were unconfirmed. Less than 24 hours after the release, three manuscripts were withdrawn following errors, and other manuscripts were corrected. [claim:03-c3]

[Visual: More than 700 neutral document icons appear; approximately half receive an “unconfirmed” label based specifically on OpenAI’s reported statement. Three are then marked “withdrawn.”]

This episode is not evidence that half of all AI-assisted research is wrong. It is a specific report about one mass release. It does show that polished manuscripts and high output volume do not substitute for confirmation.

A reviewer speaking in a SciSpace webinar makes the normative point plainly: AI should help produce good research, not merely more research. [claim:03-c4] The same reviewer tells PhD researchers that they are becoming the subject experts. That practitioner guidance is not controlled evidence, and SciSpace has a commercial interest in AI-mediated research workflows. But the advice fits the responsibility attached to authorship: expertise must remain visible in the decisions and checks.

[Visual: Counter slows down beside “paper volume”; a checklist fills beside “research quality.”]

What should an author preserve? Not a supposed transcript of the model’s hidden thought process. Preserve the auditable lineage available to you: prompts when materially relevant, retrieved sources, source passages, code and parameters, test outputs, rejected alternatives, changed assumptions, and human approval points. In a Latent Space interview, Periodic Labs describes recording conversations, intuitions, laboratory actions, computations, and code to capture the process of science rather than only its final output. That is the company’s account of its approach, not independent validation. [claim:03-c5]

Detailed logging also has limits. Confidential peer review, participant privacy, cybersecurity, and proprietary data may prohibit retaining or disclosing some material. Disclosure rules vary across journals and institutions, and the supplied evidence does not establish one universal threshold for reporting AI use. Researchers must follow the policies that apply to the specific venue and project.

The combined evidence supports a practical standard: neither fluent rationales nor polished manuscripts demonstrate faithful reasoning, verification, or human contribution. Responsible AI-assisted authorship requires an auditable link from claims to evidence and from major decisions to an accountable researcher. [claim:03-c5]

You may delegate tasks. You may not delegate the obligation to verify, disclose where required, correct unsupported claims, and defend the work carrying your name.
